title: Gowanus
summary: Gowanus is a Brooklyn placename for the historic creek, bay, and locality recorded in early Dutch colonial records as Gowanus, Gowanes, and Gouwanes.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Canarsie Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: Although Gowanus is a deeply familiar neighborhood name to modern Brooklyn residents, its origins as a traditional Indigenous place name for the lands stretching down to Bay Ridge are frequently overlooked. Acknowledging the Native roots of such everyday locations reveals how the foundational geography of Long Island was established and named long before European settlement.
introduction_content: Gowanus is the traditional placename for lands that spanned present-day Gowanus to the north down to Bay Ridge.
history_content:
A colonial purchase on already cultivated Native land

A report held by the NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission describes Bennet and Bentyn’s 1636 purchase of about 930 acres at Gowanus from Canarsee people. The landscape already included generations of Native maize cultivation. Dutch settlement followed on a lived-in and worked homeland, not unused ground.

The existing shaded Gowanus area supplies geographical context. It is not a reconstruction of that 930-acre deed: its edges must not be read as the limits of the transaction.

Alyssa Loorya, Eileen Kao and Elissa Rutigliano, Phase IA Documentary Study and Archaeological Assessment for the Ficesco Sites, August 2021, revised May 2024, printed p. 18 (PDF p. 23), Regional History—Seventeenth Century. NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission archive.

Venison and oysters at Gowanus, 1679

On the evening of September 29, 1679, Jasper Danckaerts reached Gowanus. His host, Symon, served a thirty-pound haunch of venison he had bought from Native people for three and a half guilders in seawant, or wampum, and a pail of Gowanus oysters, “the best in the country,” some not less than a foot long. Settlers burned the shells for lime and shipped pickled oysters to Barbados.

Journal of Jasper Danckaerts, 1679–1680 (1913), printed pp. 53–54, entry for September 29, 1679.

Robert Grumet’s study of the journal adds that Danckaerts watched a man fall into a trance during a dance at Gowanus and wake to tell the gathering what menitto, the spirits, had told them.

Robert S. Grumet, New World Encounters: Jasper Danckaerts’ View of Indian Life in 17th-Century Brooklyn (Brooklyn: The Brooklyn Historical Society, 1986), exhibition catalog: Brooklyn place identities, archaeology, Danckaerts’ observations, “The Brooklyn Indian Diaspora” and Brooklyn’s Native community.

A Mohawk neighborhood in North Gowanus

In the twentieth century, Mohawk ironworkers from Kahnawake and their families lived just north of here. Robert Grumet placed their community in North Gowanus; Brooklyn Public Library describes it in today’s Boerum Hill. Read more at Little Caughnawaga.

Robert S. Grumet, New World Encounters: Jasper Danckaerts’ View of Indian Life in 17th-Century Brooklyn (Brooklyn: The Brooklyn Historical Society, 1986), exhibition catalog: Brooklyn place identities, archaeology, Danckaerts’ observations, “The Brooklyn Indian Diaspora” and Brooklyn’s Native community.

Brooklyn Public Library, Brooklynology, “Brooklyn Mohawks,” November 24, 2009: Little Caughnawaga’s boundaries, the Paul Diabo case, Cuyler Presbyterian Church, and the community’s size and decline.
translation_content:
Recorded forms include Gowanus, Gowanes, and Gouwanes. The available Tooker text is truncated before a full variant list or secure translation, so the meaning remains uncertain.

Why Place Names Matter

“A place is given a name ‘for something important about it in the past,’ and the name later becomes a ‘window into intimate history.’”

— Kay Muhr, Place-Names of Northern Ireland (2007), quoted in Library of Congress symposium report

Although Gowanus is a deeply familiar neighborhood name to modern Brooklyn residents, its origins as a traditional Indigenous place name for the lands stretching down to Bay Ridge are frequently overlooked. Acknowledging the Native roots of such everyday locations reveals how the foundational geography of Long Island was established and named long before European settlement.
